text.p: Eddo Brandes hammered the final nail into England's coffin on their disastrous tour of Zimbabwe as the visitors slumped to a 131-run defeat in the final one day international on Friday.

Brandes, a chicken farmer affectionately known to his friends as Chicken George, took a hat-trick on his way to a career best five for 28. England were bundled out for 118 against Zimbabwe's 249 and lost the series 3-0.
The only thing that went right for England was when Mike Atherton won the toss at the Harare Sports Club. But he made the wrong decision and sent Zimbabwe into bat.
Opening batsman Grant Flower set the hosts on their way with a fluent 62 from 87 balls and his brother Andy raced to 35 from 30 balls.

But the quality knock came from Atherton's opposite number Alistair Campbell who finished 80 not out from 102 balls with four fours and a last over six off Craig White. Zimbabwe finished at 249 for nine -- a good but not unbeatable total on a flat pitch.

But Brandes turned the game on its head between the fourth and sixth overs. The 33-year-old outswing bowler had Nick Knight caught down the leg side for three off the last ball of the fourth over, his second over of the match.

After Alec Stewart had hit a boundary in the next over, bowled by John Rennie, Brandes tore the innings to shreds. He trapped John Crawley plumb lbw for a golden duck and then had Nasser Hussain brilliantly caught behind by Andy Flower with the hat-trick ball.
It was the 11th hat-trick in one day international cricket and the first against England.
Wisely Campbell opted to bowl Brandes through and he obliged by having Stewart (29) and Atherton (18) caught behind on his way to the second best return by a Zimbabwean in one day internationals.

At the end of Brandes' spell England were 59 for six and the match was effectively over. Heath Streak dismissed all rounders Ronnie Irani and Craig White for the third and fourth ducks of the innings and Paul Strang had Darren Gough caught slogging for seven to make the score 77 for eight.
Some last-ditch hitting from Alan Mullally (20) and Robert Croft (30 not out) saw England past their lowest ever score in one-day cricket -- 93 all out against Australia at Leeds in 1975.
But at the end of the day England had reached rock bottom and Zimbabwe cricket had been placed well and truly on the map.
